sections.h2: Who sells and who buys in Miami
sections.html:
Miami has an estimated 489,812 residents across 36.00 square miles of land, up 10.8 percent from 2020, and only 30.8 percent of its 194,821 households own their home. Most sellers here own into a market of renters and investors. About 77.2 percent of residents speak another language at home, so expect bilingual showings and have any contract translated or explained before anyone signs.

A citywide midpoint hides a wide spread between a waterfront condo and an inland bungalow, so get an offer for your own address.

Rarely allowed. The city's short-term rental rules treat houses and duplexes in T3 and T4-R transect zones as generally not eligible for short-term rental or lodging use, and tie that position to City of Miami v. Airbnb.

Converting apartments and condos faces a longer checklist: a Certificate of Occupancy, a state lodging license, a Certificate of Use, a Business Tax Receipt and any county approvals. The Certificate of Use renews yearly and the city may audit or inspect without notice. Once more than 25 percent of units are in short-term use, the whole building is classed as transient, which triggers a change of occupancy and extra building code work.

Check zoning with the city before you count on nightly income as an alternative to selling.

sections.h2: Does Miami-Dade's recertification rule apply to my property?
sections.html:
Not to a single family house. Single-family homes, duplexes, and buildings with an occupant load of ten or less and 2,000 square feet or less are outside the process. It matters mostly to condo and apartment owners.

For covered buildings, the program began in 1975 and was amended June 1, 2022 after a state law on milestone inspections of condominium and cooperative buildings of three stories or more. Coastal condo buildings of that height within three miles of the shoreline built on or after 1998 are inspected at 25 years, other newer buildings at 30, and each repeats every ten years.

  • The owner receives a Notice of Required Recertification.
  • Within ninety days of the notice, a written report from a Florida-registered engineer or architect must be filed.
  • The report certifies the structure is structurally and electrically safe for continued occupancy.

A condo seller should have the building's recertification status in the document package.

Only Miami-Dade runs its own formula: 60 cents per hundred dollars plus a 45 cent surtax, with the surtax skipped on a document that transfers only a single-family dwelling. Every other county charges 70 cents.

The base counts any mortgage that stays on the property, so a payoff does not shrink it. All parties on the instrument are liable regardless of who the contract names, so read that clause slowly.

  • Clerk recording charges under section 28.24 of the Florida Statutes.
  • Payoffs for mortgages, judgments and unpaid taxes.
  • A draft settlement statement you review before signing.

sections.h2: Miami-Dade tax calendar and your closing
sections.html:
Value and billing sit in separate county offices. The property appraiser neither mails bills nor collects money, so any question about a balance owed goes to the Tax Collector.

The 2026 roll was certified October 16, 2026, and the June 1 estimate of countywide taxable value was $540.7 billion, up 5.5 percent over 2025. A challenge to value is filed with the clerk inside a 25-day window that opens with the proposed tax notice, and the value adjustment board hears it.

Whoever buys a homestead house is taxed on full market value from the next January 1 forward, which can mean a noticeably higher bill than you paid. If you buy again in Florida, you can request portability with the new homestead filing, due March 1.

A cash sale can still close if each issue is cleared or priced in. A title search surfaces mortgages, judgments and unpaid tax, and a bill still open after April 1 is delinquent with certificates sold by June 1.

Older buildings often hide open or missing permits. Ask the city's building department what is open on your parcel, then ask the buyer whether the offer takes the work as is.

  • Inherited house: the estate may need a court order before anyone can convey title, and summary administration exists for smaller estates.
  • Past-due mortgage: ask the lender for the payoff and case status in writing.
  • Tenant in place: three days' written demand for unpaid rent, weekends and court holidays excluded, or 30 days' notice to end a monthly tenancy.

sections.h2: What happens after the deed is signed?
sections.html:
The clerk of court records it and takes the stamp tax while the title company clears liens. Quitclaim, warranty, special warranty and trustee's deeds are all taxable, so changing the form does not change the result.

The appraiser's site promotes a free clerk alert that emails you soon after any deed or other paper lands on your parcel. Sign up before and after a sale to see what gets filed, and keep the settlement statement with your tax records.

sections.h2: Help from the Miami-Dade appraiser's office
sections.html:
The office runs two public branches, downtown and in Cutler Bay, with appointments online, plus neighborhood outreach events where staff review values, exemptions and portability one on one. Widow, widower and disability exemptions can be filed online with uploaded documents, and agricultural classification applications are online too. Staff also take reports of suspected homestead exemption fraud.

Before pricing, look up your parcel's exemptions and assessed value and bring the printout to any offer discussion.

sections.h2: How to judge a cash offer
sections.html:
Weigh the offer against a listing's take-home once commissions, repairs and the months of upkeep are subtracted. In the contract, find who pays the stamp tax, title policy and recording, and what happens to the deposit.

Get the closing date and closing agent in writing, and do not sign the deed until the contract is final. Pay no fee just to receive an offer. If you are unsure, request a second offer and compare terms line by line.

sections.h2: Steps for a Miami cash sale
sections.html:
The usual order is a written offer, a signed contract, a title search, a review of the settlement statement and a signing. Bring photo ID, your payoff letter and your latest tax bill. If you own a condo, ask the association for its estoppel letter and the building's recertification status early, since both can take time.

If you rent the property out, tell the buyer whether the lease stays in place, and hand over the deposit and the rent roll at closing. After the deed is recorded, the closing agent pays off liens and sends you the balance.

faqs.q: Is Miami's deed tax higher than elsewhere in Florida?
faqs.a: Its formula differs: 60 cents per hundred dollars plus a 45 cent surtax, but the surtax does not apply when only a single-family dwelling is transferred. Other counties charge 70 cents.

faqs.q: Can a Miami single-family house be a short-term rental?
faqs.a: Generally no for houses and duplexes in T3 and T4-R zones. Verify your zoning with the city before building a plan on nightly rent.

faqs.q: Does recertification apply to a Miami single-family home?
faqs.a: No. The county exempts single-family homes, duplexes and small buildings of 2,000 square feet or less with ten or fewer occupants.

faqs.q: Who sends my Miami property tax bill?
faqs.a: The Miami-Dade Tax Collector. The Property Appraiser sets value and exemptions but does not mail bills.

faqs.q: Does my reduced assessment pass to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. Cap savings belong to the seller, not the house. The buyer begins at market value, and you keep savings only by porting them when you claim a new Florida homestead.
